title: 1 in 3 games in the last Next Fest disclosed AI on their Steam page. Among games with 10K+ followers: zero
author: Dream_Ep
selftext:
Next Fest is over, and a question I kept seeing during the fest was "how many games here use AI anyway?".  
So I checked the AI disclosure section of every game on Valve's official list ! :D

6,826 pages, 2,443 with a disclosure. 36%. More than 1 in 3. Honestly, with all the noise about AI on socials and the sheer number of games in this fest, I kind of saw it coming. And it’s not just Steam: This week [itch.io](http://itch.io) said it deleted “a couple terabytes of AI slop” and added a “No AI” filter to its search.

But according to datas it's really not spread evenly. Under 50 followers before the fest, 40% of games disclose AI. Between 200 and 499 it's 16%. Between 2K and 10K, 13%. Above 10K followers: 0 out of 28. Not a single one.

![img](r2qdwdfndfzh1)

By genre it's a pretty clean split. Board games (58%), turn-based strategy (55%), economy (53%) and card games (52%) are the most AI heavy tags. At the bottom: platformers (16%), precision platformers (19%) and "Funny" (21%). Cozy is low too, 26%.

My guess:  
in a card or strategy game the systems are the game, and art is the part a solo coder can't do. In a platformer the art and the feel are the game. And cozy players, well, they're the ones who check.

Small print:  
only the top 5 tags of each game, broad ones like Indie or Action left out, tags with 100+ games. No game names.

Next time:  
what they actually use it for. Spoiler, it's mostly art, but there's some funny stuff in there.

I'm building NextWishlist, a tool that tracks this kind of stuff for your own game and its niche every day. Link in the comments if you're curious ;)

I'm curious do you use any ai, and for what? And do you have an explicit disclosure on your page?

replies.body: I think it is 100% now. Coz even if they personaly don't, the tools and software they use probably did at some point

replies.author: i_rate_slop
replies.body:
Eh. The problem is with the disclosure.

I generate my UI with code. I generate my assets with code. I generate my sound effects with code.

So either make me disclose code or remove the disclosure entirely because it serves no purpose for people that put even a small amount of effort into their work to circumvent the wording of the disclosure.

And part of the problem is that people put in low effort and it’s obvious it’s AI generated, but they’re technically following the rule.

replies.author: Lyefyre
replies.body: Since the sound is something that people can hear, I'd say disclose that sounds have been AI generated. In the end, nobody cares if it was created by code or not.

replies.author: i_rate_slop
replies.body:
I think the distinction between a trained model producing sounds and me coding a system to produce sounds is actually critical to the discussion.

If a tool I use being coded with AI means all downstream assets are also AI generated, well then I suppose soon everything is AI generated.

The whole concept of disclosure is flawed with the exception of audio and visuals with the intent to be perceived as reality. Like an assistant shouldn’t pose as a real human without disclosure.

replies.author: ledniv

replies.author: Neither_Berry_100

comments.author: supimjay
comments.body: Do you think there’s some bias here, games with longer lifecycles and more community building are going to have a bigger following? While ai devs are generally newer devs iterating much quicker.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
Yeah, very likely part of it, good point.   
  
Older pages had more time to build a following, and AI devs are probably newer on average. I tried to check page age but I can only date a small part of the pages, so I can’t separate the two properly.   
So I’d read it as “the big games mostly don’t disclose”, not “AI keeps your game small”.

replies.author: supimjay
replies.body: What are the games in the biggest bucket? It’s a pretty small list, we could probably just sample it manually and pull a few to get an idea

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
I looked, and it pretty much backs your point. Of the 28, at least 17 had their Steam page up for over a year before the fest, and 6 are sequels or licensed games from known publishers. 24 already had a public demo before the fest. So mostly established projects with a long runway, which fits the “time and community” explanation better than anything about AI...!

I’d rather not list names though, the thread is already playing “guess who’s hiding AI” and I don’t want to throw specific games under the bus. They’re all on the public Next Fest list if you want to dig :D

replies.author: Neither_Berry_100
replies.body: One problem with AI games is it makes things too easy so the devs are not likely to put in quality effort anywhere.

replies.author: supimjay
replies.body: Sure but that wouldn’t explain why no games are in the top bucket which I think is the more interesting metric here.

It definitely helps explain it.

I also haven't seen anything fantastic vibe coded yet. Only the odd claim of making some money.

comments.author: MrMegaPhoenix
comments.body:
I’m dumb but what does this mean?

People don’t care if if uses AI?

Or the “popular enough” games didn’t have any AI?

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
Not dumb at all, I should’ve been clearer!   
  
It’s the second one: the bigger a game was before the fest (in Steam followers), the less likely it was to have an AI disclosure. 40% of the tiny games had one, 13% between 2K and 10K followers, and 0 of the 28 games above 10K.

Whether people care is another question, and I’m looking at it in a later post (did the label cost them followers during the fest?).   
  
Spoiler, the answer surprised me ;)

comments.author: Plants-Matter
comments.body:
The only thing this objectively proves is that disclosing AI usage will likely have a negative effect on the game's popularity. 

A lot of assumptions can be made from the data, some more reasonable than others. 

I guarantee there are a non-zero amount of AI games with 10K+ followers. They just didn't disclose their AI usage, forcing people to judge the game on the merits of the game itself rather than what tools were used.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
Careful with that one, I don’t think it proves that. It shows that big games rarely disclose, but it could go the other way: AI devs are often newer and smaller, so they start with fewer followers. The data can’t tell which causes which.

I actually looked at whether the label cost games followers during the fest itself, comparing games of the same size. Coming in a later post, and the result wasn’t what I expected haha ! ;)

replies.author: Plants-Matter
replies.body:
I'll keep an eye out for your follow up post. 

Considering the rabid demands for a "no AI" filter in Steam, it seems intuitive that disclosing will affect popularity. The unknown part is how large that group actually is. Reddit makes it seem like a large group, but I suspect it's a vocal minority. 

I'd really love to see an A/B test of the same game released with and without an AI disclosure, but it would be impossible to conduct that experiment properly.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
Yeah a real A/B test would be the dream, but you can’t release the same game twice haha. Comparing games of the same size during the same fest is the closest I could get, and even that has holes (page age, studios not disclosing...)

On the vocal minority part, honestly no idea either. [itch.io](http://itch.io) just added a “No AI” filter to its search, so if they ever share how many people actually turn it on, that would answer it better than any Reddit thread :D

Can we draw a conclusion that not declaring AI can potentially lead to higher success?

If a developer isn't using AI at this point to speed up development, either they've been developing their game for 4-5 years or they're braindead.

replies.author: Dream_Ep

Nope, I don’t think you can draw that one. Big games were big before the fest, and most of them have been around for years, so the label isn’t what made them successful. And yeah, “no disclosure” definitely doesn’t mean “no AI”, the data only shows who puts the label on the page.

What I could test is whether the label hurt games of the same size during the fest.   
  
That’s coming in a later post, stay tuned :D

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
There are two conclusions you can draw from this. One, devs of low quality games overwhelming use AI and devs of high quality games don’t. Two, most devs use AI and those with existing reputation or producing high quality work hide the use well and avoid disclosing it. Given that games is a big business, money is on the line, and AI dramatically reduces costs and time, I’m betting on the second conclusion.

I don’t want to sound like a conspiracy theorist, but I’m honestly starting to wonder if AAA studios are fueling anti AI rhetoric because it penalizes small studios and indies who aren’t able to hide AI use well.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body: Honestly I think it’s probably a mix of both, and the data can’t tell them apart, it only sees the label. On the AAA theory I have zero data, so I’ll stay out of that one haha

comments.author: redskeletonbarbarian

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
The distinction in this moment matters more for AI-developed games, though. Toggling the filter is about virtue signalling, not about consumer preference (...we could argue about how much virtue signalling is, in fact, a form of consumer preference, and if we were to do that, I'd just concede the point; the average Itch game consumer is not toggling that switch for the same reason they'd toggle a pixel art switch or a genre switch. They're toggling it because they've been instructed that it is the morally righteous thing to do). 

Since AI development is not in any way tied to the player experience, hiding it is entirely possible and plausible, as are finding loopholes to technically say you didn't use AI to build \[X\] or \[Y\] feature. If I just use AI for tooling, and then use the tooling to make the game, has AI built anything? Not by the strictest standards, and since the consumer can't tell either way, why label the product? 

The filter will encourage developers who do not want to be filtered to dodge it, because AI usage isn't player-facing and can only be discovered through investigation.
